# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (100) must cover the tallest glyph plus its outline. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:
  eight offsets across one refresh, 3 s each, the step number stamped on the
  screen, filmed at 120 fps. 3.2 to 9.5 ms had no vanished line in 39 updates;
  1.1 and 15.8 ms did, with the seam at film row 495 and film row 268: about 107
  film rows per millisecond (the camera frame is taller than the panel; the
  466-row panel scans about 28 rows per millisecond), so the bad window is only
  about 5 ms wide. It is valid for a full-frame push (the 20.6 ms copy). A push
  of another size moves the flush and the sweep would have to be repeated: the
  QR overlay's 328-row push is one, so a seam may show while the code is up.
  `-DTE_DIAG` logs the TE period and where pushes start.
- `te_sync.c` trusts few edges. Once it knows the period it accepts a rising
  edge only within period/16 of a whole number of periods since the last, so a
  missed edge or a stray pulse cannot move the lock; four misfits in a row drop
  the lock and relearn it. An edge further ahead than one period is stale (the
  32-bit microsecond counter can pass half its range with the line dead), and
  waiting stops 100 ms after the last edge. The ISR is placed in IRAM, but
  Arduino's pin dispatcher and `gpio_get_level` are in flash; that is safe only
  because `CONFIG_ARDUINO_ISR_IRAM` is unset. The run log's `sync=` is the wait
  for the edge and is left out of `push=`: compare `push=` across hacks, and add
  `sync=` to get the frame's latency.
- Reading a film of the display: iPhone slo-mo files store their first and
  last seconds at normal speed, so the label changes every ~100 frames there
  and every 360 in the 120 fps middle. Stabilise against the scenery (four
  corner patches; a mask edge around the display pins phase correlation at
  zero), level the rows, and count a vanish only when a line is missing across
  at least three 24 px windows on one row and not in a settled frame of the
  same update. A detector that finds nothing must also find the event you know
  is there: mine reported zero until a known vanish was used as a control, and
  reported many false events on steep line stretches until settled frames were.
- Every push also dims the screen: the dimmest band falls to 0.86 of its
  settled brightness for about 25 ms (three camera frames at 120 fps), at 5 Hz,
  with or without TE sync (0.860 synced, 0.870 unsynced). It is probably the
  "whole screen redraws" flicker. Its cause is not known. Rod sees no dimming
  with the sparser build (20 rows of 50 points, a step of about 91 ms against
  165), so it may track how much is lit or how long the copy runs; not yet
  filmed (issue #68).
- A hack's returned delay is waited after the push, and only the push counts
  against it, so its own step adds to the frame time: to hold a rate, return
  the target minus the step (`ad_flyingtoasters.c`: 19.5 fps became 28.9).

  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat

# X11 shim and framework gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse`, whose `double` maths is software on the S3. A
  test pins the pixels to `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  The older wrappers (Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame, Substrate) have not been
  checked.
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); a bitmap or `None`
  draws nothing, and only `XCopyArea` writes into a bitmap (`XCopyPlane`
  follows the same rule). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). The `logo_180`/`360`
  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
  lines, so they still take the stroker. Issue #56 asks whether the stroker's
  gaps and overpaint touch them. Changing shared stroke code can move their
  pinned frames: ask Rod.
- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
  are pinned with the original.
- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`
  -> `XPutPixel` -> `XPutImage` keeps the pixel; `XPutImage` does not swap.
  Only `lowrez_put_image` swaps, because Fireworkx writes ordinary RGB565
  bytes straight into the image data) and
  `ImageByteOrder`; `CoordModePrevious` in `XFillPolygon`, `XDrawLines` and
  `XDrawPoints`; `XCreatePixmapFromBitmapData` (X bitmap data is least
  significant bit first); a spline of our own (`spline.c`, not xscreensaver's);
  `XQueryColor`; `DisplayOfScreen` (the display opened last); the fill-rule,
  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).
- Added for the third batch, each test-first: `ya_random` (the C library's
  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with
  `create_xshm_image`, `put_xshm_image` and `destroy_xshm_image`, which are a
  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page
  keysym constants (X's values; no key event ever arrives); and `glOrtho` (see
  `gl.md`). The Edit tool drops a trailing space from `old_string` and
  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).
- `allocate_alpha_colors` still finds no colour planes, so a hack that wants
  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
  allocate any color planes" on the host.
- The comment in `xshim.h` saying `XPutImage` byte-swaps a 16-bit image has
  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.

content.text:
Pacman's dirty arrays cost about 19 KB of payload on the host, and I haven't yet confirmed how much of that sits in internal heap on the device. The number is exact; what it means for internal heap is an estimate.

I wrote a scratch program (in the scratchpad, not the repo) that runs Pacman for 50 frames and walks the shim's list of live pixmaps.

| | Pacman | Truchet (for contrast) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colour pixmaps (each a `Canvas`) | 120 | 1 |
| Rows across them | 4,740 | 866 |
| Pixel data | 518,520 B | 1,499,912 B |
| Dirty arrays (4 B per row) | **18,960 B** | 3,464 B |
| Depth-1 bitmaps (no `Canvas`, no dirty arrays) | 42 | 0 |

- **What the dirty arrays cost:** Pacman's sprites are small, about 4.3 KB each. The dirty arrays add about 3.7% on top of their pixel data. That is 240 extra `malloc` calls (two per pixmap), and the allocator's per-block overhead on the S3 probably adds a few KB beyond the 19 KB. I haven't measured that part.
- **Against the internal heap:** about 19 to 23 KB out of the roughly 318 KB free while Truchet runs, so around 6 to 7%. Note that 318 KB was measured under Truchet, not Pacman.
- **Not measured:** the same small-pixmap point applies to the pixel data. If the 16 KB-style PSRAM threshold is what I think it is, most of those 4 KB sprites also live in internal heap. The arrays would then be a small slice of a much bigger internal cost. I haven't checked the threshold, so that's a guess.
- **Still needs the device:** the actual internal `heap=` before and after #64.

For the fix, the issue's first option is a small change: allocate the dirty arrays only for the window canvas and have `mark_span` do nothing when they are NULL. It means touching `canvas.c`, which every hack shares. Reading `canvas.c` and `pixmap.c`, the pixmap canvases never get their dirty rows read, but I'd confirm that with a test first.

Rod, do you want the fix now on the strength of the host numbers (about 19 KB is real but modest), or should #65 wait for a device measurement? I'd lean towards doing the fix test-first, since it's cheap and removes 240 small allocations. Otherwise I'll move on to #56.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown
text

- item

text
```

**Heading:**

```markdown
text

## Head

text
```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```lang
code
```

text
````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

When in doubt:

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only
7. Two trailing spaces = line break

import math

W = 30
HALF = W / 2
CX = CY = 100.0


def arc_points(x, y, w, h, n):
    cx, cy = x + w / 2, y + h / 2
    rx, ry = w / 2, h / 2
    pts = []
    for i in range(n):
        a = 2 * math.pi * i / (n - 1)
        pts.append((round(cx + rx * math.cos(a)), round(cy - ry * math.sin(a))))
    return pts


n = math.ceil(2 * math.pi * 80 / 2) + 1
pts = arc_points(20, 20, 160, 160, n)
if pts[-1] == pts[0]:
    pts.pop()
m = len(pts)
dedup = [pts[0]]
for p in pts[1:]:
    if p != dedup[-1]:
        dedup.append(p)
pts = dedup
m = len(pts)


def direction(a, b):
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    ln = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    return dx / ln, dy / ln


def seg_quad(a, b):
    ux, uy = direction(a, b)
    nx, ny = -uy * HALF, ux * HALF
    return [(a[0] + nx, a[1] + ny), (b[0] + nx, b[1] + ny),
            (b[0] - nx, b[1] - ny), (a[0] - nx, a[1] - ny)]


def join_poly(prev, at, nxt):
    d1, d2 = direction(prev, at), direction(at, nxt)
    dot = d1[0] * d2[0] + d1[1] * d2[1]
    cross = d1[0] * d2[1] - d1[1] * d2[0]
    if abs(cross) < 1e-4 and dot > 0:
        return None
    side = -1.0 if cross > 0 else 1.0
    n1 = (-d1[1] * side, d1[0] * side)
    n2 = (-d2[1] * side, d2[0] * side)
    v = at
    p1 = (v[0] + n1[0] * HALF, v[1] + n1[1] * HALF)
    p2 = (v[0] + n2[0] * HALF, v[1] + n2[1] * HALF)
    k = HALF / (1 + dot)
    tip = (v[0] + (n1[0] + n2[0]) * k, v[1] + (n1[1] + n2[1]) * k)
    return [v, p1, tip, p2]


def inside_convex(poly, px, py):
    """Signed margin: positive = inside; min over edges of signed distance."""
    best = 1e9
    area = sum(poly[i][0] * poly[(i + 1) % len(poly)][1]
               - poly[(i + 1) % len(poly)][0] * poly[i][1]
               for i in range(len(poly)))
    sgn = 1 if area > 0 else -1
    for i in range(len(poly)):
        a, b = poly[i], poly[(i + 1) % len(poly)]
        ex, ey = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
        ln = math.hypot(ex, ey)
        if ln == 0:
            continue
        d = sgn * (ex * (py - a[1]) - ey * (px - a[0])) / ln
        best = min(best, d)
    return best


def report(px, py):
    print(f"pixel centre ({px},{py})")
    rows = []
    for i in range(m):
        a, b = pts[i], pts[(i + 1) % m]
        q = seg_quad(a, b)
        d = inside_convex(q, px, py)
        rows.append((abs(d) if d < 0 else 0, d, f"seg {i} {a}->{b}"))
        prev, nxt = pts[(i - 1) % m], b
        jp = join_poly(prev, a, nxt)
        if jp:
            d = inside_convex(jp, px, py)
            rows.append((abs(d) if d < 0 else 0, d, f"join {i} at {a} prev {prev} next {nxt}"))
    covered = [r for r in rows if r[1] >= 0]
    print("  covered by", len(covered), "polygons")
    near = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: abs(r[1]))[:6]
    for _, d, label in near:
        print(f"  margin {d:+.6f}  {label}")


for px, py in [(57.5, 31.5), (25.5, 137.5), (57.5, 168.5)]:
    report(px, py)

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and its
  `assert()` aborts on a failed allocation, and it ran at 1.2 fps, so it is
  shelved (issue #37): its source stays in `firmware/src/hacks/celtic/`, it is
  not in `g_hacks[]`, and `failed_ports.txt` lists it. A failed port that has
  its source and a measured row still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed
  standalone. Measure on the device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` stops with "hypnowheel: does not compile ... 'rotator.h'
  file not found": a dropped GL port counts in the backtest and is probed
  standalone, without the GL helpers' include path. `docs/speed-backtest.md`
  was last regenerated before Hypnowheel was ported, and was not regenerated

input.content:
Posted by Claude, working for Rod (commit `3c634ad`, host only, nothing
flashed, nothing committed).

## Pacman: not affected on this board

- Pacman's `wallwidth` is `(xs + ys) >> 4`, with a minimum of 1. At 466 px
  the cell size is about 11, so the width is 1 and the walls take the old
  thin-line path, not the wide stroker. A zoomed frame at 1000 steps shows
  clean one pixel walls and corners.
- The wide stroker would only be reached at a cell size of 16 or more.
- Pacman's frames at 100, 1000 and 4000 steps are byte-identical with and
  without the fix below.

## The gap: float rounding on a shared edge

The empty pixel at (57, 31) is not the miter joins, the point spacing or
the quad geometry. Round joins leave no gaps, but miter and bevel leave the
same eight pixels, so it is the tiling of segment quads and join wedges.

- At each gap the pixel centre lies exactly on an edge shared by a segment
  quad and the join wedge at its end vertex. That happens where the arc's
  rounded points step diagonally, because a 45 degree edge passes through
  pixel centres.
- `fill_convex` takes a pixel when its centre is right of the left edge and
  at or left of the right edge. On row 31 the segment quad's right edge
  should be exactly 57.5, but float32 gives 57.499996185, so
  `floorf(xr - 0.5f)` drops pixel 57. The wedge's left edge is exactly 57.5,
  which correctly excludes it. Both polygons reject the pixel.
- A new test, `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band`, fails on
  `main` with 8 empty pixels in the 67 to 93 band.

## A candidate fix, not applied

Adding a small tolerance to the right edge, `floorf(xr - 0.5f + 1e-3f)`
in `fill_convex`, makes the new test pass. The full native suite then
fails only on pinned frames. A temporary change to the pin loop (reverted)
listed every moved hash:

- Moved: Deluxe, Forest, Rotor, Compass.
- Unmoved: Pacman, Braid.

I have not looked at the moved frames, and the pins stay as they are until
Rod has said to change them.

## Celtic: heavy overpaint

Celtic is not registered, so this was a scratch build of `celtic.c` with the
shim's `stroke.c` counting each `canvas_fill_rect` call and the pixels it
writes. Over 60 steps, per step:

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Fills per step | about 500 at the start, 5,000 to 24,000 later |
| Paints per distinct pixel | about 40 to 57 |
| Most paints on one pixel | up to 218 |

Whole run: 817,434 fills painted 5,249,093 pixels onto 114,335 distinct
pixels (summed per step), a ratio of 45.9. That is the Deluxe pattern
(about 25 paints per pixel there). Each fill is a row of about 6 pixels,
so call overhead counts as well as the overpaint.

Not done: the step split on the device, which needs a flash.

I've finished the host-side work on #56 and posted the findings as a comment: <https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/56#issuecomment-6113817610>. Nothing is committed, nothing was flashed, and `stroke.c` is back at HEAD.

**Pacman is not affected.** `wallwidth` is `(xs + ys) >> 4`, which comes out at 1 on this board, so the walls take the thin-line path and never reach the wide stroker. A zoomed frame shows clean one-pixel walls and corners. Pacman's frames at 100, 1000 and 4000 steps are also byte-identical with and without the fix below.

**The gap's cause is float rounding.**
- Every empty pixel sits exactly on an edge shared by a segment quad and a join wedge, where the arc's rounded points step diagonally.
- On row 31, `fill_convex` computes the quad's right edge as 57.499996185 instead of 57.5, so `floorf(xr - 0.5f)` drops pixel 57. The wedge's left edge is exactly 57.5, which correctly excludes it, so both reject the pixel.
- It isn't the miter joins, the point spacing or the quad geometry. Round joins leave no gaps, and miter and bevel leave the same eight.
- A failing test, `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band`, is in the worktree and uncommitted. It fails on `main` with 8 empty pixels.

**Celtic overpaints heavily.** I built it as a scratch program on the host, since it isn't registered. Each step paints about 40 to 57 times per distinct pixel, with a worst pixel painted up to 218 times. That is the Deluxe pattern at roughly twice the ratio. Steps run to 5,000 to 24,000 tiny fills. The step split on the device still needs a flash.

**The candidate fix.** I haven't applied it. Adding a `1e-3f` tolerance to the right edge in `fill_convex` makes the new test pass, and it changes one line of shared code (the patch is in the scratchpad as `eps_fix.patch`).
